newsitem.title: USA: BNCCORP sees Q2 loss due to loan provision.
newsitem.headline: BNCCORP sees Q2 loss due to loan provision.

text.p: BNCCORP Inc said Tuesday it expected to report a loss of about $570,000 or $0.24 per share for the second quarter due to a one-time, extraordinary $1.9 million increase in its loan loss provision.

The increased provision resulted from the allegedly questionable loan practices by a recently dismissed employee, it added. Without the provision, BNCCORP said it anticipated record earnings of about $660,000 or $0.28 per share for the quarter compared to $439,000 or $0.19 a year ago.
It expects to announce results by the end of July.
BNCCORP, a bank holding company, said the increase in the loan loss provision resulted from a routine internal audit of a subsidiary bank's loan portfolio.
More than 80 percent of the $1.9 million provision is attributable to questionable activity with one customer, it said.
BNCCORP said it terminated the loan officer responsible for the loans in question and will aggressively pursue legal and other actions to seek to minimize any loss to the company.
Those steps include possible civil litigation, pursuing a claim with its fidelity bond carrier and cooperating with law enforcement authorities investigating this matter.
"We are reviewing all of our loan policies and procedures," Tracy Scott, chairman, said in a statement.
BNCCORP said about $1,900,000 was placed in reserve of which approximately $900,000 -- all relative to one customer -- will be charged off for the second quarter.

"We are optimistic that indemnity should eventually recover most of the loss but there's no guarantee," Gregory Cleveland, president, said. "That's why we increased our loan loss provision. However, due to the current situation regarding the borrowers and the likelihood of litigation, an extended period of time will probably be required to resolve this matter."
BNCCORP said its balance sheet remains strong and future positive earnings growth is expected as total deposits increase and net interest margins improve, coupled with continued steady loan growth.
